\tutwhat{Open-loop CSTR START-UP transient with OpenFOAM-style real-time instant dirs: charged cold (320 K), no control, watch T(t) and the holdup approach the natural steady state by scrubbing 0/ 50/ 100/ ... s}
\begin{tutnarrative}
Process: A continuous CSTR (first-order compA $\to$ compB, mild exotherm) is CHARGED cold (320 K, pure compA) and then left to run with NO controller. The jacket sits at a fixed 320 K. From the cold start the reactor warms a little from the reaction exotherm, the feed/ outlet convection competes, and (T, composition) relax to the natural open-loop steady state over \textasciitilde{} several residence times.

What this tutorial shows: The OpenFOAM-style transient solution directories. The case root fills with REAL-TIME directories `0/ 50/ 100/ ... 1000/`, each with the layout of 0/: `<t>/internalStates/reactor` is the reactor HOLDUP at that instant, `<t>/feed` and `<t>/product` the two streams. Scrub the times and you watch T(t) and the inventory march to steady state --- the same way you scrub a CFD transient in ParaView.

To compare CLOSED-LOOP control, see ctrl01\_cstr\_temp\_control (a PID drives T to a 350 K setpoint) and ctrl05\_disturbance\_transient (a PID rejecting a feed-temperature disturbance), both also writing time dirs.

\end{tutnarrative}

\tutwhat{Tanks-in-series RTD: three equal mixing tanks chained by the ctrl router; impulse in tank 1 $\to$ Erlang-3 response at tank 3 (tbar = 3 tau, sigma2/tbar2 = 1/3), Levenspiel closed forms as anchors.}
\begin{tutnarrative}
the SECOND HALF of the RTD lesson, unlocked by the ctrl router (ruled 2026-08-24): three EQUAL mixing tanks in series, each tau = n/F = 0.004/5e-5 = 80 s, chained by the same `in`/`outputs` topology grammar every steady flowsheet already uses. The router applies each connection ONE-STEP-EXPLICITLY: at every accepted driver step the downstream tank integrates on the upstream outlet at the step's START -- a transport delay of one driver step (1 s here, against tau = 80 s), announced by the [routing] lines at startup.

THE EXPERIMENT. The tracer impulse is an INITIAL-CONDITION substitution in tank 1 only (compB 0.0002 of the 0.004 kmol holdup -- substitution, not addition, so every tank holds exactly tau = 80 s and the closed forms are exact). An initial holdup m in tank 1 is mathematically a perfect impulse into tank 1 at t = 0, so tank 3's outlet is the Erlang-3 density:

E(t) = t\textasciicircum{}2 e\textasciicircum{}(-t/tau) / (2 tau\textasciicircum{}3) tbar = 3 tau = 240 s sigma2 = 3 tau\textasciicircum{}2 = 19200 s\textasciicircum{}2 (sigma2/tbar2 = 1/3 exactly) peak at 2 tau = 160 s (visible in trajectory.csv)

Levenspiel, Chemical Reaction Engineering, ch. 14 (the tanks-in-series model): the variance ratio 1/N is THE diagnostic the lesson teaches -- one tank gives 1, three give 1/3, a PFR gives 0. ctrl18 is the N = 1 control; this case is N = 3 on identical tanks.

WHAT THE ANCHORS TOLERATE, stated: the engine measures moments by trapezoid on the accepted 1 s grid and truncates at 1600 s (= 20 tau of one tank); both effects are far inside the anchor bands, and the router adds a one-step transport delay per connection (2 s total on tbar's 240 s -- inside the 1 \% band, and the honest price of an explicit scheme, stated rather than hidden).

\end{tutnarrative}

\tutwhat{Feed-and-bleed NF start-up: the loop concentrates from the feed's to its steady value, the module solved quasi-steady at every instant}
\begin{tutnarrative}
the START-UP of the feed-and-bleed loop whose steady state is membrane18\_nf\_feed\_and\_bleed.

THE PLANT. Fresh feed (1 wt \% glucose, 200 kmol/h) joins the recycle in MIX and fills a 1 m3 recirculation tank; the tank feeds an NF270 module (15 m2); the retentate is split, 95 \% back to MIX and 5 \% bled off. The permeate and the bleed leave. At t = 0 the tank holds feed.

WHAT IS SOLVED HOW. The TANK is a vessel (dynamicCSTR, no reaction, no jacket): it holds an inventory and is integrated in time. MIX, NF and SPLIT hold essentially no liquid, so on the loop's time scale they are at steady state at every instant -- each is its steady unit wrapped as `quasiSteady` and re-solved on every accepted state. The module the run solves is exactly the one membrane18 solves; only the time around it is new.

WHAT TO WATCH. The tank starts at the feed concentration, so the module first sees the feed and delivers its single-pass flux. As the retentate returns, the loop concentrates, the osmotic pressure rises and the flux falls towards the value membrane18 reports at steady state. The time scale is the tank's contents over the flows that carry solute OUT of the loop -- the bleed, and the permeate because NF270 passes glucose partly: V / (Q\_bleed + Q\_permeate (1 - R)) is about 1 m3 / 5.3e-4 m3/s = 1900 s, and the loop is faster than that (measured e-folding about 1340 s, from successive gaps in balanceTrajectory.csv) because the bleed leaves at the RETENTATE concentration, richer than the tank's. 6 h is some 16 of them, so the end state must be membrane18's: the golden holds the module's flux, rejection and the permeate and bleed flows to membrane18's own within 2e-5. That agreement is the case's anchor -- a transient that does not end on the steady answer is wrong.

WHAT IS ASSUMED, and printed on the run: the quasi-steady units hold no inventory (nothing accumulates in the module or the pipes), the tank is well mixed, and the loop's pressure is the module's feed pressure throughout (no pump is modelled, as in membrane18 -- see its header). The first law is NOT claimed: the dynamic ledger needs a stored energy functional per unit, which the quasi-steady adapter does not provide, and the run says so rather than closing it with a zero.

\end{tutnarrative}

\tutwhat{Feed-and-bleed UF start-up: the loop concentrates the protein, and the gel-limited flux falls as ln(c\_g/c\_b) while it does}
\begin{tutnarrative}
ultrafiltration of a protein in a feed-and-bleed loop, from start-up.

THE PLANT. 1 m3/h of a 10 kg/m3 BSA solution joins the recycle in MIX and fills a 0.5 m3 recirculation tank; the tank feeds the UF module of membrane19 (5 m2, 3 bar, the same hypothetical membrane and gel parameters); the retentate is split, 80 \% back to MIX and 20 \% bled off. At t = 0 the tank holds feed.

WHAT IS SOLVED HOW. The TANK is a vessel (dynamicCSTR, no reaction, no jacket), integrated in time, and DECLARED isothermal (`energy isothermal;`): BSA carries no heat capacity, so the tank cannot solve an energy equation, and here nothing would move T anyway -- every stream is at 298.15 K with no reaction and no jacket. MIX, UF and SPLIT hold essentially no liquid and are each a steady unit wrapped as `quasiSteady`, re-solved at every accepted state -- the module is membrane19's, law and all.

WHAT TO WATCH -- the lesson of gel polarisation IN A LOOP. The module is gel-limited, so its flux is k ln(c\_g/c\_b) whatever the pump does (membrane19 shows the plateau). The loop returns the retained protein, the tank concentrates, c\_b rises -- and the flux FALLS with it, as a logarithm, until the protein leaving in the bleed and the permeate balances the protein fed. MEASURED on this case: the module's mean flux falls from 3.30e-5 m/s (119 L/(m2 h)) at start-up to 2.88e-5 m/s (104 L/(m2 h)), 13 \% less, while the tank goes from 10 to 15.3 kg/m3 of protein, with an e-folding time of about 2500 s -- so a plant sized on the FEED's flux is short of area by that 13 \%. 6 h is some 8 time constants. Every <t>/ directory the run writes holds each stream's state and the tank's holdup at t (open 600/ against 21600/), and the module's own J\_w\_avg rides trajectory.csv as a kpi column.

EVERY UF NUMBER HERE IS HYPOTHETICAL, as in membrane19 (the membrane, c\_gel, S, k\_film -- read its header); BSA's MW is derived from its UniProt sequence. The shape is the lesson, never a number. NOT MODELLED: the first law (BSA carries no enthalpy datum, and the quasi-steady adapter claims none), a pump, fouling in time.

\end{tutnarrative}

\tutentry{unsteady05\_tank\_valve\_drain}{tutorials/unsteady/unsteady05\_tank\_valve\_drain}
\begin{tutscheme}
\begin{tikzpicture}[>={Stealth[length=2mm]}, every node/.style={font=\scriptsize}]
  \node[draw, rounded corners=2pt, align=center, minimum width=1.9cm, minimum height=0.85cm, fill=black!4] (tank) at (0.0,-0.0) {\textbf{tank}\\[-1pt]{\tiny dynamicTank}};
  \draw[->] ($(tank.west)+(-1.05,0.00)$) -- ($(tank.west)+(0,0.00)$) node[at start, above, font=\tiny, anchor=south west] {feed};
  \draw[->] ($(tank.east)+(0,0.00)$) -- ($(tank.east)+(1.05,0.00)$) node[at end, above, font=\tiny, anchor=south east] {drain};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{tutscheme}
\tutwhat{Water tank drained through a valve, no controller: after a 50 \% step in the inflow the level SELF-REGULATES to the closed-form h$\ast$ = (Q/(Cv x))\textasciicircum{}2/g (0.998 m $\to$ 2.245 m)}
\begin{tutnarrative}
A water tank drained through a valve, with NO controller. The inflow steps from 0.20 to 0.30 kmol/s (a 50 \% step, applied at t = 0 by starting the tank at the steady level of the OLD inflow and feeding the NEW one -- the initial-condition step of unsteady02), and the level climbs to a new steady level by itself, because the outflow grows with the level:

Q = Cv x opening x sqrt(dP / rho) [m3/s] dP = P + rho g h - P\_downstream (static head + vessel pressure - downstream) F\_out = Q rho / MW [kmol/s] A rho/MW dh/dt = F\_in - F\_out (mass balance, the level is volume / area)

Here the vessel is open to the same pressure the valve discharges to (P = P\_downstream = 1 atm), so the head alone drives the flow and the steady state F\_out = F\_in has a closed form:

h$\ast$ = (Q / (Cv x))\textasciicircum{}2 / g with Q = F\_in MW / rho

Cv is the valve's effective flow AREA in m2 (the orifice equation's Cd A), `opening` the fraction of the stroke (linear), the outlet is at the bottom. Because Q \textasciitilde{} sqrt(h), h$\ast$ grows with the SQUARE of the inflow: a 1.5-fold step in the inflow gives a 2.25-fold step in the level (0.998 m $\to$ 2.245 m at rho = 1001.55 kg/m3, the package's own density at 293.15 K: the water record's Vliq at 25 C with Rackett supplying the temperature shape). The engine prints this closed form at start-up; the run's own final level, read from trajectory.csv (column `level`), agrees with it to < 1e-3.

WHAT TO SEE. A first-order-like response with tau \textasciitilde{} 2600 s at the new level (linearising Q about h$\ast$: tau = A / (dQ/dh) = 2 A h$\ast$ / Q). Compare with ctrl21: with a manipulated OUTFLOW instead of a valve the same tank has NO such tendency -- it integrates the difference of the flows without bound, and only a level controller closes the loop.

ENERGY. The tank stores H on the elements datum (the package's mixture liquid surface) and T is a readout; the feed arrives at the tank's own temperature, so T stays at 293.15 K and the first-law ledger closes (see the `[balance]` lines and check\_dynamic\_tank).

\end{tutnarrative}

\tutentry{unsteady06\_reactor\_fill\_and\_react}{tutorials/unsteady/unsteady06\_reactor\_fill\_and\_react}
\begin{tutscheme}
\begin{tikzpicture}[>={Stealth[length=2mm]}, every node/.style={font=\scriptsize}]
  \node[draw, rounded corners=2pt, align=center, minimum width=1.9cm, minimum height=0.85cm, fill=black!4] (reactor) at (0.0,-0.0) {\textbf{reactor}\\[-1pt]{\tiny dynamicCSTR}};
  \draw[->] ($(reactor.west)+(-1.05,0.00)$) -- ($(reactor.west)+(0,0.00)$) node[at start, above, font=\tiny, anchor=south west] {feed};
  \draw[->] ($(reactor.east)+(0,0.00)$) -- ($(reactor.east)+(1.05,0.00)$) node[at end, above, font=\tiny, anchor=south east] {product};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{tutscheme}
\tutwhat{A reactor that starts as a heel and FILLS while a first-order isomerisation runs: volume and level follow the holdup, n\_A(t) = F/k + (n0 - F/k) exp(-kt) in closed form}
\begin{tutnarrative}
a reactor with a LEVEL fills from a heel while it reacts (C205, slice 2: dynamicCSTR with `volumeMode variable`).

The constant-volume dynamicCSTR cannot start empty: its volume is a number you type and F\_out = F\_in. Here the liquid inventory is the state, the volume is derived from it on the case's package and the level is that volume over a declared vertical cylinder (D = 0.5 m, H = 1.0 m):

dn\_i/dt = ndot\_in,i - F\_out x\_i + sum\_r nu\_i r\_r V V = sum n\_i MW\_i / rho(T, P, x) h = V / (pi D\textasciicircum{}2 / 4)

The outflow is DECLARED: `mode flow`, F\_out = 0, so the vessel only fills. Feed: pure isobutanol, F = 1.0e-3 kmol/s, k = 4.0e-4 1/s (constant: Ea = 0), starting from a 0.02 m heel. An isomerisation changes no moles, and a first-order law makes the extent rate k n\_A independent of the volume, so the mole numbers have an EXACT closed form while the volume keeps growing:

n\_A(t) = F/k + (n\_A0 - F/k) exp(-k t) n\_B(t) = n\_A0 + n\_B0 + F t - n\_A(t) M(t) = M0 + MW F t (both isomers have the same MW) V(t) = M(t) / rho h(t) = V(t) / area c\_A = n\_A / V

check\_dynamic\_cstr\_level recomputes these from the declared numbers and holds the run to them (the density is the run's own column: it moves a little with T, because the isomerisation is mildly exothermic).

ENERGY. Both species carry a formation datum, so the vessel takes the CANONICAL route (announced at start-up): it stores H on the elements datum, the heat of reaction is a consequence of it, the outlet term cancels, and the ledger CLAIMS mass and energy and closes. Compare ctrl22, the same reactor with a level loop and a temperature loop together.

\end{tutnarrative}
\tutreadme{dynamicCSTR with volumeMode variable (D = 0.5 m, H = 1.0 m) starts from a heel (0.02 m of isobutanol at 300 K, an "empty" vessel --- exactly zero is refused by name), is fed 1.0e-3 kmol/s of pure isobutanol, has no outflow, and isomerises it to 2-butanol with a first-order law, k = 4.0e-4 1/s (Ea = 0, so k cannot move with the small temperature rise). 1500 s, 5 s steps; runs under choupoSemiContinuous (no controller).}
\tutreadme{1. The closed form. The reaction changes no moles and its extent rate k$\cdot$n\_A does not depend on the volume, so the mole numbers are exact: n\_A(t) = F/k + (n\_A0 - F/k)$\cdot$exp(-kt), n\_B = n\_A0 + n\_B0 + F$\cdot$t - n\_A. The volume is V = M(t)/? with M(t) = M0 + MW$\cdot$F$\cdot$t, and the level is V over the 0.196 m$^2$ cross-section. The run reproduces all of them to \textasciitilde{}4e-9 (check\_dynamic\_cstr\_level recomputes them). 2. The rate uses the current volume. A first-order law cannot show it; the gate runs a second-order variant (r$\cdot$V = k$\cdot$n\_A$^2$/V) against an independent integration --- a vessel that kept the heel's volume in the rate would be off by 73 \%. 3. The ledger claims mass and energy and closes (\textasciitilde{}1e-14): the canonical route is announced at start-up (the vessel stores H on the elements datum; the heat of reaction is a consequence of it). 4. Change outflow \{ F 0.0 kmol/s; \} to 0.5 and the heel runs dry in the first step (RAN DRY); set endTime to 4000 and it overflows. Both are refused by name, never clamped.}
\tutreadme{The same reactor under a level loop and a temperature loop is ctrl22\_reactor\_level\_and\_temperature.}

\tutentry{unsteady07\_fast\_tank\_full}{tutorials/unsteady/unsteady07\_fast\_tank\_full}

\tutwhat{Two tanks in series, a big one and a small one, BOTH integrated in time: the outlet after a step in the feed, the full model the reduced twin unsteady08 is compared with}
\begin{tutnarrative}
two mixing tanks in series, a BIG one and a SMALL one, and the question every model of a plant meets: does the small one need to be integrated at all?

THE PLANT. A feed of 1e-3 kmol/s runs through SLOW (1 kmol held, time constant tau\_s = 1000 s) and then FAST (0.05 kmol held, tau\_f = 50 s). Both tanks start full of compA; from t = 0 the feed is pure compB, the tracer. No reaction, no jacket: the two synthetic components (the unsteady02 pair, 30 kg/kmol each) carry nothing but their identity.

THE FULL MODEL (this case). Both tanks are vessels (`dynamicCSTR`), each integrated in time, so the outlet of FAST lags the outlet of SLOW by about tau\_f. Its twin unsteady08\_fast\_tank\_reduced replaces FAST by its quasi-steady relation -- a tank that holds nothing that accumulates, so its outlet IS its inlet -- and the two answers differ by that lag alone. The ratio of the two time scales is

eps = tau\_f / tau\_s = 0.05,

and the largest gap between the two outlet tracer fractions is, in closed form for these two linear tanks,

x\_full(t) - x\_red(t) = tau\_f (e\textasciicircum{}(-t/tau\_s) - e\textasciicircum{}(-t/tau\_f)) / (tau\_s - tau\_f),

whose maximum is eps\textasciicircum{}(1/(1-eps)) = 0.0428 here. The EduTool page "When the fast obeys the slow" runs both cases with the small tank's holdup changed and draws that gap against eps.

WHAT THE STEP COSTS. The router hands SLOW's outlet to FAST once per driver step (one-step explicit, announced by the [routing] line), so the driver step must stay short against tau\_f: 0.25 s is a 40th of the smallest tau\_f the page uses (10 s), and the fixed RK4 step is stable only below 2.785 tau\_f. The reduced twin has no such limit from FAST.

\end{tutnarrative}
\tutreadme{Two mixing tanks in series under choupoSemiContinuous: SLOW holds 1 kmol (time constant 1000 s at the 1e-3 kmol/s feed) and FAST holds 0.05 kmol (50 s). Both start full of compA; from t = 0 the feed is pure compB. Both tanks are dynamicCSTR vessels, integrated in time. 5000 s, 0.25 s steps.}
\tutreadme{1. The lag. FAST's outlet follows SLOW's outlet about 50 s late. In trajectory.csv the tracer fraction leaving FAST is FAST.n\_compB / (FAST.n\_compA + FAST.n\_compB). 2. The reduced twin. unsteady08\_fast\_tank\_reduced replaces FAST by its quasi-steady relation (outlet = inlet). The largest gap between the two outlets is 0.0428 at the ratio of time scales 0.05, and the closed form for two linear tanks gives the same, eps\textasciicircum{}(1/(1-eps)). 3. The step. SLOW hands its outlet to FAST once per driver step, so the step must be short against FAST's time constant (the [routing] line says so).}
\tutreadme{The EduTool page "When the fast obeys the slow" runs this case and its twin with FAST's holdup changed.}

  \draw[->] (SLOW) -- (FAST) node[midway, above, font=\tiny] {s12};

\tutwhat{The same two tanks with the small one replaced by its quasi-steady relation (a storageTank wrapped as quasiSteady, outlet = inlet): the reduced model of unsteady07}
\begin{tutnarrative}
the REDUCED twin of unsteady07\_fast\_tank\_full: the same two tanks, the same step in the feed, with the SMALL tank replaced by its quasi-steady relation.

THE REDUCTION. If the small tank's time constant tau\_f is short against the big tank's tau\_s, its content follows its inlet almost at once, and in the limit it holds nothing that changes: its outlet IS its inlet. That relation is what a `storageTank` computes (outlet = inlet, plus the holdup its declared residence time implies, published as a number and never integrated), and `quasiSteady` re-solves it on SLOW's outlet at every accepted instant ("SAME INSTANT" in the [routing] line). So the engine runs ONE differential equation where the full model runs two.

WHAT IS KEPT AND WHAT IS LOST. The residence time below (50 s, the full model's tau\_f) changes no number on the outlet: it only sizes the holdup the storageTank publishes (kpi\_holdupMass\_kg, what FAST would hold if it were at steady state with its inlet). The lag of about tau\_f is what is lost, and unsteady07 measures it: the largest gap between the two outlet tracer fractions is 0.0428 at eps = 0.05, and it grows with eps.

\end{tutnarrative}
\tutreadme{The reduced twin of unsteady07\_fast\_tank\_full: the same feed step and the same big tank SLOW, with the small tank FAST written as a storageTank wrapped as quasiSteady. Its outlet IS its inlet, re-solved at every accepted instant; nothing in it is integrated.}
\tutreadme{1. One differential equation instead of two. Only SLOW carries a holdup in trajectory.csv; FAST publishes the holdup its declared residence time implies (FAST.kpi\_holdupMass\_kg), a number and not a state. 2. What is lost. The outlet is SLOW's outlet, with no lag. Against the full twin the largest gap in the outlet tracer fraction is 0.0428. 3. The routing line says SAME INSTANT for FAST: a unit with no inventory is solved on its inlet at the instant, never a step late.}
